sections.heading: 5.1 Tensorization of token embeddings
sections.text: Let X ∈ ℝ T × d X\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} be the usual input sequence (length T T , embedding dimension d d ). Fix an integer p p such that p | d p\mid d and define the slice width d s := d / p d_{s}:=d/p . 2 2 2 The clean tensorization assumes p p divides d d . If not, one may (i) choose a nearby admissible p p , or (ii) pad the embedding dimension to the next multiple of p p and truncate back after unfolding; we keep p | d p\mid d throughout to avoid cluttering notation. We reshape X X into a third-order tensor 𝒳 = Ten p ⁡ ( X ) ∈ ℝ T × d s × p , \mathcal{X}=\operatorname{Ten}_{p}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{s}\times p}, by splitting the feature dimension into p p slices: 𝒳 ( t , j , k ) := X ( t , ( k − 1 ) d s + j ) , t = 1 , … , T , j = 1 , … , d s , k = 1 , … , p . \mathcal{X}(t,j,k):=X\big(t,\,(k-1)d_{s}+j\big),\quad t=1,\dots,T,\;j=1,\dots,d_{s},\;k=1,\dots,p. In what follows, the contextual representation will be produced in tensor form, 𝒵 ∈ ℝ T × d s × p , \mathcal{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{s}\times p}, and can be unfolded back to the standard matrix representation Z = Mat p ⁡ ( 𝒵 ) ∈ ℝ T × d Z=\operatorname{Mat}_{p}(\mathcal{Z})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} when needed.

Throughout the implementation-oriented parts (LayerNorm/FFN), we focus on real orthogonal transforms (notably DCT-type transforms), so that transform-domain slices remain real-valued for real inputs. 3 3 3 In all experiments we use an orthonormal DCT (DCT-II with orthonormal scaling), so ℒ − 1 \mathcal{L}^{-1} is implemented by the corresponding inverse DCT with the same normalization. Other orthogonal transforms can be used without changing the slice-wise calculus; Fourier/DFT choices remain valid but lead to complex-valued slices (Appendix A.4 ).

sections.heading: Theorem 19 (Slice-wise equivalence of the ℒ \mathcal{L} -attention and ℒ \mathcal{L} -FFN cores) .

Then, for fixed parameters transformed by ℒ \mathcal{L} , the computations of (i) MHA ℒ ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{MHA}_{\mathcal{L}}(\cdot) and (ii) TFFN ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{TFFN}(\cdot) are slice-wise in the transform domain: for each i ∈ { 1 , … , p } i\in\{1,\dots,p\} , the corresponding output slice depends only on X ^ i \widehat{X}_{i} and the slice- i i transformed parameters, and coincides with a standard attention/FFN computation at width d s d_{s} .

sections.heading: remark 8 (LayerNorm placement and “exact equivalence”) .
sections.text: In our implementation, LayerNorm is applied after mapping back to the original tensor domain (and is computed slice-by-slice along mode-2). Because LayerNorm is nonlinear and not invariant under a general ℒ \mathcal{L} transform, the full encoder layer is not strictly separable in the transform domain. Theorem 19 therefore calibrates the exact claim to what is implemented: slice-wise equivalence holds for the attention/FFN cores, while cross-slice coupling occurs through the alternating ℒ − 1 \mathcal{L}^{-1} mixing and subsequent normalisation. Importantly, the encoder parameter scaling and the projection/FFN FLOP reductions derived from the slice-wise cores remain valid.

sections.heading: Coupling across slices.
sections.text: Although the computation is slice-wise in the transform domain, the model is not equivalent to a static partition of the embedding dimension. After each block, applying the inverse transform ℒ − 1 \mathcal{L}^{-1} mixes the p p spectral channels, so the input slices of the next layer are linear combinations of the previous layer’s slice outputs. As a result, information can propagate across slices from layer to layer through the alternating ℒ \mathcal{L} / ℒ − 1 \mathcal{L}^{-1} mappings, yielding structured cross-slice interactions even though each block is computed slice-wise in the ℒ \mathcal{L} -domain.

sections.heading: FLOPs vs. wall-clock time.
sections.text: Table 2 accounts for arithmetic cost, but measured runtime is also influenced by (i) extra memory-bound passes introduced by the DCT/IDCT steps, and (ii) kernel-launch/parallelism effects when the p p slice-wise sub-encoders are executed sequentially. With the batched parallel implementation noted after Algorithm 1 , effect (ii) is largely removed, and the remaining overhead is dominated by the transform steps and framework-level memory traffic. The standard Transformer has per-layer cost 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d 2 + T 2 ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(Td^{2}+T^{2}d) . The tensor Transformer reduces the projection and FFN terms to 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d 2 / p ) \mathcal{O}(Td^{2}/p) , while the attention terms remain 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}d) . The transform overhead 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d ​ log ⁡ p ) \mathcal{O}(Td\log p) is typically small.

sections.heading: 6.2 Fair comparison protocol
sections.text: All models share identical embedding and classifier layers; only the encoder varies. This isolates the encoder as the sole source of architectural and parameter-count differences. At small d d , the embedding layer dominates total parameters (e.g. IMDB), so encoder compression is not fully reflected as total-model compression. At larger d d , the encoder becomes a dominant fraction of parameters, so encoder compression translates into substantial end-to-end savings (Section 6.5 ).

sections.heading: Parameter-matched baseline.
sections.text: To disentangle architectural effects from pure parameter reduction, we include a parameter-matched (PM) standard baseline that approximately matches the encoder parameter count of T4 ( p = 4 p{=}4 ). Specifically, Std-1L is a single-layer standard encoder at full width d d . At d = 128 d{=}128 this yields 247,808 247{,}808 encoder parameters ( 0.250 × 0.250\times Std), closely matching T4-linear’s 254,016 254{,}016 ( 0.256 × 0.256\times ). At d = 256 d{=}256 it yields 987,136 987{,}136 encoder parameters ( 0.250 × 0.250\times Std), matching T4-linear’s 999,552 999{,}552 ( 0.253 × 0.253\times ). This comparison isolates the architectural question: at equal encoder budget, is it better to invest in a single full-width layer or in four tensor-factored layers. Table 8 shows that T4-linear consistently outperforms Std-1L on both datasets, indicating that the tensor ℒ \mathcal{L} -product structure provides more than a simple capacity reduction.
